item.title: Optimal Worst-Case Open Addressing: Braided Cuckoo Hashing
item.description: arXiv:2610.33229v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we introduce braided cuckoo hashing, an open-addressed hash table that supports load factor up to $1 - \varepsilon$ (for some parameter $\varepsilon \in (0, 1)$), while supporting queries, insertions, and deletions in worst-case time $O(\log \varepsilon^{-1})$, with high probability. This result represents an exponential improvement on insertion/deletion time over previous constructions, and disproves a conjecture of Bender, Kuszmaul, and Zhou that the product of worst-case query time and expected insertion/deletion time must be $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1})$.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Krapivin, William Kuszmaul

item.title: Approximation algorithms for identical parallel machine scheduling with assignment costs
item.description: arXiv:2610.33666v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study non-preemptive scheduling on identical parallel machines in which assigning job $j$ to machine $M_i$ incurs the cost $c_{ij}=a_iw_j+b_j$. The processing times $p_j$ and the cost weights $w_j$ are independent, and the number of machines is part of the input. For every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ and every deadline $T$ for which a schedule with makespan at most $T$ exists, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that computes a schedule with makespan at most $(1+\varepsilon)T$ whose total assignment cost does not exceed the minimum under the deadline $T$. Using this algorithm as a subroutine, we obtain a polynomial-time approximation scheme for minimizing the makespan under a total cost budget whose schedules always satisfy the budget; this answers an open question for costs $c_{ij}=l_ic_j$ with $c_j$ independent of $p_j$. For the lexicographic problem, in which the total assignment cost is minimized among all schedules of minimum makespan, we obtain in polynomial time a schedule with makespan at most $1+\varepsilon$ times the minimum and total assignment cost at most that of a lexicographically optimal schedule; this improves the makespan guarantees of earlier algorithms for additive and multiplicative costs. For costs $c_{ij}=s_i+a_iw_j$, where $s_i$ is charged for each job processed on $M_i$, the same guarantees are obtained in quasi-polynomial time.
item.dc:creator: Wei Li

item.title: Engineering Lightweight Burrows-Wheeler Transform Construction on the GPU via Prefix-Free Parsing
item.description: arXiv:2610.33889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Burrows-Wheeler transform (BWT) is the core of many compressed full-text indexes and most read aligners. The fastest BWT constructions on GPUs need about $20$ bytes of device memory per character, which severely limits the texts that can be processed there. For example, on our GPU with 24 GB device memory, this is only about 1200 MiB. Prefix-free parsing (PFP) can be used to reduce the memory requirements of BWT construction algorithms in main memory. But, it uses hash tables and inverted lists which are not suited for GPUs. We show that PFP-based BWT construction can work with only sorting, scanning, and simple data-parallel procedures. This results in our GPU construction gpupfpbwt that on an NVIDIA RTX 3090, reduces the peak memory on an English text 11.9 bytes per character. There, it can processes 2108 MiB input files, which is 1.8 times larger than what the current state of the art libcubwt can handle. It is faster than or on par with libcubwt on eight of nine repetitive texts but 2.0 to 3.2 times slower on five of six non-repetitive ones, i.e., it provides a trade-off between required device memory and throughput.
item.dc:creator: Florian Kurpicz, Maximilian Paris

item.title: Random Deletion for Circuits in Regular Matroids
item.description: arXiv:2610.33918v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a simple random deletion algorithm to find short circuits in regular matroids. Given a regular matroid $M$ with $m$ elements, the algorithm randomly deletes each element independently with probability $1-1/m^{\Theta(1/g)}$ where $g$ is the size of a minimum circuit, and returns the remaining set $R$ of elements. We establish the following results: 1. With high probability, $R$ contains no circuit and is therefore independent. 2. For every $\alpha$-approximate minimum circuit $C$ where $\alpha\geq 1$, with probability at least $m^{-O(\alpha)}$, the entire circuit $C$ survives in $R$ and moreover, the minimum number of elements that need to be removed to make $R$ independent is $O(\alpha\log(\alpha+2))$. This yields an algorithmic proof that the number of $\alpha$-approximate minimum circuits is $m^{O(\alpha)}$, improving the previous known bound of $m^{O(\alpha^2)}$ by Gurjar and Vishnoi, and resolving a recent conjecture of Khanna, Putterman, and Song. Our results yield two immediate applications. First, we obtain very simple RNC algorithms for computing the shortest circuit, and for enumerating all $\alpha$-approximate circuits, of a regular matroid without computing the Seymour decomposition. Second, we obtain a randomized parallel algorithm to find a basis of a regular matroid under independence-oracle access. It uses polynomially many independence-oracle queries in $O(\log m)$ adaptive rounds and succeeds with high probability. This follows from the framework of Khanna, Putterman, and Song and the improved counting bound, and extends their result from graphic matroids to regular matroids.
item.dc:creator: Karthekeyan Chandrasekaran, Chandra Chekuri, Weihao Zhu

item.title: New Fault-Tolerant $(\alpha,\beta)$-Spanners
item.description: arXiv:2610.33934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present new constructions of vertex fault-tolerant (VFT) $(\alpha,\beta)$-spanners with substantially improved size bounds. Given a bound $f$ on the number of vertex faults, an $f$-VFT $(\alpha,\beta)$-spanner is a subgraph of $G$ that preserves an $(\alpha,\beta)$-spanner of $G- F$ for every fault set $F \subseteq V$ with $|F| \le f$. Most existing constructions of VFT $(\alpha,\beta)$-spanners rely on a black-box sampling technique that incurs an exponential blow-up compared to their non-fault-tolerant counterparts. We develop two independent techniques for constructing $f$-VFT $(\alpha,\beta)$-spanners that improve the dependence on $f$, reducing it to polynomial overhead. For every unweighted graph $G=(V,E)$ on $n$ vertices, stretch parameter $k$, and fault parameter $f$, we show: (i) $f$-VFT $(O_{\epsilon}(k^{\epsilon}), O_{\epsilon}(k))$-spanners with $\tilde{O}(f^{exp(1/\epsilon)}\cdot n^{1+1/k})$ edges for any $\epsilon \in (0,1)$. For any fixed constant $\epsilon$, this introduces a $poly(f)$ overhead compared to the non-faulty constructions of [Ben-Levy and Parter, SODA 2020] and [Chechik and Lifshitz, SODA 2026]. (ii) For any $\delta \in (0,1)$, an $f$-VFT $\left(O_{\delta}(\sqrt{k}),O_{\delta}(k) \right)$-spanner of size $\tilde{O}(f^{1+\delta} \cdot n^{1+\frac{1}{k}})$. Hence, it incurs a size overhead of only $f^{1+\delta}$ compared to the above-mentioned non-faulty analogs. (iii) $f$-VFT $(k,k-1)$ spanner of size $O(k^3 \cdot f \cdot n^{1+\frac{1}{k}})$, nearly matching the lower bound $\Omega(f^{1-\frac{1}{k}}n^{1+\frac{1}{k}})$ known for $f$-VFT $(2k-1,0)$ spanners by [Bodwin et al., SODA 2018]. The first result is obtained via a new adaptation of the Baswana--Sen framework to the VFT $(\alpha,\beta)$ setting. The other two bounds follow from a highly involved analysis of a natural extension of the fault-tolerant greedy spanner.
item.dc:creator: Merav Parter, Elizaveta Popova, Elad Tzalik

item.title: A Nearly Optimal Min-Cut Algorithm for Dynamic Streams
item.description: arXiv:2610.34097v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give an $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon)$-space algorithm for the minimum cut problem in dynamic streams, resolving the space complexity of streaming min-cut up to polylogarithmic factors. Ding, Garces, Li, Lin, Nelson, Shah, and Woodruff (ITCS 2025) obtained the same $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon)$ space bound for insertion-only streams, while prior to our work the best known bound even for unweighted dynamic streams was $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^2)$, due to Ahn, Guha, and McGregor (PODS 2012). Our main technical contribution is an $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon)$-space for-each cut sketch in dynamic streams, which may be of independent interest. The construction applies to weighted graphs under general $\pm\Delta$ updates, a stronger model than the standard dynamic-stream setting in which weighted edges are inserted and deleted in their entirety. Despite this stronger guarantee, our algorithm is surprisingly simple and relies on very little machinery. We also obtain applications to minimum $\ell_p$-norm $k$-partitioning for every fixed $k$, weighted correlation-clustering evaluation for two clusters, and for-each cut sketching in balanced directed graphs.
item.dc:creator: Yang P. Liu, Hoai-An Nguyen, Vihan Shah, David P. Woodruff

item.title: Bicriteria Approximate Navigable Graphs in General Metrics
item.description: arXiv:2610.34302v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study approximation algorithms for constructing sparse navigable graphs in general metrics. Given an $n$-point metric $(P,d)$ and a parameter $\alpha\ge 1$, an $\alpha$-navigable graph is a directed graph $G=(P,E)$ such that for every ordered pair of distinct points $s,t\in P$, the vertex $s$ has an outgoing edge $(s,p)$ with $d(p,t)<d(s,t)/\alpha$. The objective is to minimize the number of edges. Approximation algorithms for this problem were recently studied by Khanna, Padaki, and Waingarten (SODA 2026), and independently by Conway et al. (SODA 2026). These works show that the single-criterion problem faces a Set Cover barrier: an $O(\log n)$-approximation is achievable, whereas obtaining an $o(\log n)$-approximation is NP-hard. To obtain faster algorithms, Khanna, Padaki, and Waingarten introduced bicriteria approximation, in which the output graph is required to be $\alpha$-navigable, while its size is compared against that of an optimal $\beta$-navigable graph for some relaxed parameter $\beta \ge \alpha$. They gave a fast matrix-multiplication-based algorithm that computes an $(\alpha,2(1+\varepsilon)\alpha)$-bicriteria $O(\log n)$-approximation in time $\widetilde O(n^\omega \log \Delta/\varepsilon)$, where $\Delta$ denotes the aspect ratio and $\omega$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. Our main result is a simpler near-quadratic-time algorithm with stronger bicriteria guarantees. For every constant $\alpha\ge 1$, we compute in time $\widetilde O(n^2\log\Delta)$ an $\alpha$-navigable graph that is simultaneously an $(\alpha,2\alpha+O(1))$-bicriteria $O(1)$-approximation and an $(\alpha,\alpha+O(1))$-bicriteria $O(\log n)$-approximation. We complement the algorithm with a hardness result showing that for every constant $\eta\in(0,1)$, no polynomial-time algorithm can compute an $(\alpha,2\alpha-\eta)$-bicriteria $o(\log n)$-approximation unless $P=NP$.
item.dc:creator: Hongyi Chen, Tianyi Zhang

item.title: Tight Coreset Bounds for Euclidean $(k,z)$-Clustering
item.description: arXiv:2610.34373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the optimal coreset size for Euclidean $(k,z)$-clustering, where $z\ge1$ is fixed. Huang, Li, and Wu (STOC 2024) proved a lower bound of $\Omega_z(k\varepsilon^{-z-2})$ for $\varepsilon\gtrsim_z k^{-1/(z+2)}$, matching the known upper bound up to polylogarithmic factors. For $0<\varepsilon<k^{-1/(z+2)}$, the upper bound $\widetilde O_z(k^{(2z+2)/(z+2)}\varepsilon^{-2})$ remained unmatched. The previous lower bounds gave only $\Omega_z(\max\{k\varepsilon^{-2},k^{(2z+3)/(z+2)}\varepsilon^{-1}\})$. We close this gap by proving a matching lower bound throughout $0<\varepsilon<k^{-1/(z+2)}$, including arbitrarily small $\varepsilon$. Together with known bounds, this determines the optimal worst-case coreset size as $$ \widetilde\Theta_z\!\left(\min\left\{k^{(2z+2)/(z+2)}\varepsilon^{-2},\,k\varepsilon^{-z-2}\right\}\right) $$ for every integer $k\ge1$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$. In particular, the bounds are $\widetilde\Theta(k^{4/3}\varepsilon^{-2})$ for $k$-median when $\varepsilon<k^{-1/3}$, and $\widetilde\Theta(k^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-2})$ for $k$-means when $\varepsilon<k^{-1/4}$. Our construction uses projection levels to encode four-wise independent signs, allowing $k$ centers to detect omissions regardless of how the retained points are reweighted.
item.dc:creator: Junqiu Hu, Lingxiao Huang, Jian Li, Baoduo Xu

item.title: Online Discrepancy of Sparse Random Vectors over Long Horizons
item.description: arXiv:2610.34410v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study online vector balancing for independent sparse random vectors: each arrival is supported on a uniformly random set of $s$ of the $n$ coordinates, with nonzero entries equal to one (binary model) or independent random signs (signed model), and an online algorithm must sign each vector upon arrival. The prefix discrepancy is the largest $\ell_\infty$-norm of the signed sums up to the horizon $T$, the terminal discrepancy that of the sum at time $T$. For binary inputs with $2\le s\le n/2$ and $T=\Theta(n)$, Altschuler and Tikhomirov showed that both are of order $\sqrt{s}+\log\log n$; they asked how the prefix discrepancy depends on the horizon and whether a matching terminal bound holds at every prescribed time. Over long horizons, the two differ. For every fixed $s\ge2$ and $c>0$, every online algorithm, even a randomized one that knows the horizon, incurs with high probability prefix discrepancy $\Omega(\log\log n+(\log T/\log n)^{\alpha_s})$ for $n\le T\le e^{cn}$, where $\alpha_s=(2^{s-1}-1)/(2^s-1)$. For $s=2$, quadratic Greedy matches this bound; for fixed $s\ge3$, we give an online algorithm with prefix discrepancy $O(\log\log n+(\log T/\log n)^{1/2})$. In contrast, a deterministic algorithm that knows neither the horizon nor the failure probability keeps the terminal discrepancy $O_k(\sqrt{s}+\log\log n)$ at each prescribed time, with failure probability $n^{-k}$ for every fixed $k$, for $2\le s\le n/2$ (binary model) and $2\le s\le n$ (signed model); for $s=2$, quadratic Greedy itself does so. This answers their terminal question, and the same order is optimal for prefixes at all polynomial horizons $T\ge n$. The lower bound uses a finite safety game realized within the input law; the upper bounds use moments of elementary symmetric polynomials and, at terminal times, a $\cosh$ potential or a translated gauge with a Foster inequality at every state.
item.dc:creator: Nicola Wengiel

item.title: Coordinating Boundaries: Improved Approximation Algorithms for Unweighted Non-Preemptive Throughput Maximization
item.description: arXiv:2610.34656v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study unweighted nonpreemptive throughput maximization: given jobs with processing times, release times, and deadlines, schedule a maximum-cardinality subset on identical machines. For every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, we give randomized algorithms with expected approximation ratios $17/13+\varepsilon$ in polynomial time and $21/17+\varepsilon$ in pseudopolynomial time. These improve the respective $4/3+\varepsilon$ and $5/4+\varepsilon$ guarantees of Armbruster, Grandoni, Tinguely, and Wiese [STOC'26]. Both results hold for an arbitrary number of identical machines. Our algorithms build on their configuration-LP and matching framework, which partitions time into blocks. For a job whose window meets multiple blocks, its boundary blocks are the first and last such blocks. Crossing boundary pairs, whose endpoints strictly interleave, permit additional assignments to sampled execution slots, while a noncrossing family can be coordinated using consistent joint distributions on at most three blocks. The exchange analysis accounts for fractional job assignments that must be erased before inserting an additional job. For the pseudopolynomial implementation, we project configurations onto selected job identities and use separate configuration distributions with common placement marginals. This retains efficient pricing while enforcing the correlations needed for coordination.
item.dc:creator: Weitian Tong, Yao Xu

item.title: Linear Hashing Is Poissonesque
item.description: arXiv:2610.34750v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Poisson approximation theorem states that when $m$ balls are tossed uniformly and randomly into $n$ bins, the distribution of the bin loads can sometimes be approximated by $n$ independent Poisson random variables of mean $m/n$. We show that when the balls are tossed via a random $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear map, the load distribution is still governed by this Poisson distribution, albeit in a (necessarily) weaker manner. This allows us to show that a random linear map behaves like a fully random map in the following ways: 1. $\textbf{Expected loads.}$ We show that the expected value of the $r$th largest bin is governed by the $r$th largest value among $n$ independent Poisson random variables of mean $m/n$. Specializing to the canonical setting of $m=n$ and $r=1$, our bounds show that the expected maximum load when $n$ balls are hashed into $n$ bins by a random $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear map is no more than the corresponding expectation for a fully random map $\textit{plus}$ $\frac{3}2 + o(1)$. Specializing to $m\gg n\log n$, we show that the expected max load is $(1+o(1))m/n$ in this regime. 2. $\textbf{Concentration.}$ When $m\gg n\log (1/\rho)$ balls are tossed into $n$ bins randomly, we expect with $0.99$ probability that $\textit{every}$ density-$\rho$ subset of bins will contain a $(1\pm o(1) )\rho$-fraction of the balls. We show that this remains the case if the $m$ balls are tossed using a random linear map, and our bound matches the $o(1)$-factor produced by the fully random case. This gives a stronger version of the Leftover Hash Lemma for linear maps. An implication of this is that all bins have load $m/n \pm O(\sqrt{(m/n)\log n})$ with probability $0.99$. We obtain these results by showing that the average of a log-potential on the bin loads is upper bounded by the cumulant generating function of a Poisson random variable of mean $m/n$.
item.dc:creator: Vinayak M. Kumar

item.title: When is greedy exact for weighted minimum 3-cut?
item.description: arXiv:2610.34851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The greedy algorithm for minimum 3-cut splits a global minimum-weight cut and then the cheaper of its two sides; it is a tight $4/3$-approximation. We show that it is exact, from every global minimum-weight cut, whenever some optimal 3-partition has two parts joined by total weight at least the weighted edge connectivity $\lambda$. This extends both theorems of Hochbaum and Shmoys from unweighted planar graphs to all weighted graphs, recovers the $4/3$ bound, and generalizes to minimum $k$-cut with a one-paragraph proof. The remaining hard instances have all pair weights below $\lambda$; for them we prove a merge lemma for Gomory-Hu sides. Finally, we give a 7-vertex graph with a unique Gomory-Hu tree whose unique optimal 3-partition contains no side of that tree, so the first stage of Kapoor's algorithm does not suffice on its own. The main theorem, the 4/3 bound, the merge lemmas and the counterexample are verified in the Lean 4 proof assistant.
item.dc:creator: Armando Rodado Amaris

item.title: Order-selection Prophet Inequality (Almost) Goes I.I.D
item.description: arXiv:2610.34892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the order-selection prophet inequality. A gambler knows the distributions of independent nonnegative random values, chooses the order in which to inspect them, and may irrevocably accept at most one value, at the time it is revealed. Since the order is irrelevant when the values are i.i.d., no algorithm can guarantee more than the optimal i.i.d.\ ratio $\Gamma_\star\approx0.74544$ of the expected maximum. We give an algorithm with competitive ratio $0.74500001$, less than $4.5\times10^{-4}$ below this bound. The algorithm samples independent arrival times and uses item-dependent thresholds. It is designed so that, conditional on its value, every item is selected with probability equal to a fixed fraction of its probability of being the maximum. We show that the constructions of this form that apply one local rule to every item are exactly those given by an allocation kernel, that is, by a coupling of two uniform random variables. Requiring every rarely winning item to follow the optimal i.i.d.\ threshold path singles out a baseline kernel, for which we prove analytically a ratio $\Gamma_0\approx0.7389$, defined through a one-dimensional control problem. Our final kernel perturbs this baseline, and its guarantee combines analytic estimates with a rigorous computer-assisted certificate.
item.dc:creator: Bo Peng, Zhihao Gavin Tang

item.title: From Linear to Polylogarithmic: Dynamic Submodular Maximization over Matroids
item.description: arXiv:2610.35131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of submodular maximization under a matroid constraint. In this problem, there is a monotone submodular function $f: 2^{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+$ and a matroid $M(N, I)$, accessible via value and independence oracles and the goal is to find the independent set $S \in I$ maximizing the objective function, i.e., $f(S) = \max_{I \in I} f(I)$. In the fully dynamic setting, the active ground set $N \subseteq N$ evolves through element insertions and deletions. The goal is to maintain a solution $S \subseteq N$ with $S \in I$ and $f(S) = \max_{I \subseteq N,, I \in I} f(I)$ after each update. Two approximation algorithms have been proposed to solve this problem: D\"utting et al. developed a $(4+\epsilon)$-approximation algorithm with an expected amortized update time of $O\!\bigl(\frac{k^2}{\epsilon} \log k \log n \log^3 \frac{k}{\epsilon}\bigr)$, and Banihashem et al. achieved a similar approximation with a better update time $O\!\bigl(k \log k \log^3 \frac{k}{\epsilon}\bigr)$. However, these methods both become inefficient when the rank $k$ of the matroid is large (e.g., when $k = n^{o(1)}$). The central open question in this line of work is whether a fully dynamic algorithm with polylogarithmic update time exists. We resolve this question by presenting the first fully dynamic algorithm for submodular maximization over matroids with polylogarithmic update time. Our algorithm maintains a $(4+\epsilon)$-approximate solution with expected amortized update time $poly(\log n, \epsilon^{-1})$, where $n = |N|$. In particular, the update time is independent of the matroid rank $k$, thereby eliminating the dependence on $k$ and settling the open problem.
item.dc:creator: Kiarash Banihashem, Samira Goudarzi, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi, Peyman Jabbarzade, Morteza Monemizadeh

item.title: Improved Quasi-Polynomial-Time Approximation for Maximum Independent Set
item.description: arXiv:2610.35228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a deterministic quasi-polynomial-time algorithm for the maximum independent set problem. If an $N$-vertex graph contains an independent set of size $2^{-t}N$, where $t$ is an integer with $1\le t\le\sqrt{\log N}/12$, then our algorithm finds an independent set of size $2^t$ in time $N^{O(t)}$. This gives an approximation ratio of $N/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log N})}$ in time $N^{O(\sqrt{\log N})}$, improving on the approximation ratio $N/2^{\Omega((\log N)^{1/3})}$ obtained by Lovett [Lov26]. A limitation of this form of analysis follows from the integrality gaps of Tulsiani [Tul09]. These gaps imply that a universal guarantee of the form $\operatorname{Las}_{R(t)}(G)\ge2^{-t}N\Longrightarrow\alpha(G)\ge2^t$, at $2^{o(\sqrt{\log N\log\log N})}$ levels, cannot hold over a range extending beyond $t=O(\sqrt{\log N\log\log N})$. Thus, the exponent $1/2$ is the limit of this form of analysis, up to a factor of $\sqrt{\log\log N}$.
item.dc:creator: Zhao Song

item.title: Computation-Friendly Compression of Matrices: Speeding up Linear and Boolean Algebra
item.description: arXiv:2610.35362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large sparse matrices---adjacency matrices of web and social graphs, feature matrices of machine-learning pipelines, the relations of graph databases---are routinely compressed to save space. Classical compressors, however, force the matrix to be decompressed before it can be used, so the space savings often yield a computational overhead. A recent line of work studies \emph{computation-friendly} compression: formats that are not only small, but let us carry out matrix--vector products, and in some cases matrix--matrix products, sums and closures, directly on the compressed representation {\em in time proportional to that compressed size}. This survey organizes that literature around the kind of redundancy each format exploits: spatial clustering of the nonzeros ($k^2$-trees and their variants), similarity between rows (Boldi--Vigna-style referencing and set-difference compression), repeated substrings (grammar compression), and dense bipartite substructures (bicliques). For each family we describe the representation, the algorithms, the theoretical guarantees and the empirical performance. Further, we show that the last three families are instances of a single general scheme, which we call a {\em sparse straight-line factorization} of the matrix, whose forward and backward substitutions evaluate right and left products in time proportional to the size of the representation, and that the product of two such factorizations is again one, which gives matrix--matrix products with a compressed output. An appendix reviews formats that must be decompressed (at least partially) before operating, for completeness. We close with a cross-family comparison and a list of open problems.
item.dc:creator: Gonzalo Navarro

item.title: Query Complexity of Learning Axis-Aligned Partitions
item.description: arXiv:2610.35495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work establishes the query complexity of learning high-dimensional boxes in the exact query learning setting. Let $X \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a set of $n$ points, labeled by a collection of $k$ boxes: the label of each point in $X$ is determined by the unique box containing it. A learner aims to exactly recover the labels for every point in $X$ given access to a label oracle. We consider three increasingly-structured settings. In the most general setting, there are no conditions on the boxes, and they may overlap. We show that CAL (Cohn-Atlas-Ladner 1994), a classical active learning algorithm, is minimax-optimal with query complexity $\Theta(kd \log (n/kd))$. When the boxes are disjoint, we examine two regimes. In the large-$k$ regime, CAL remains minimax-optimal. For the constant-$k$ regime, an optimized variant of the Halving algorithm (Heged\"{u}s 1995) can beat CAL by a $\log(d)$ factor. Finally, in the most-structured settings, the boxes correspond to the leaves of a constant-sized decision tree. We prove a tight query complexity of $\Theta(d + \log n)$ that is additive in $d$ and $\log n$, generalizing a recent result (Black-Larsen-Mazumdar-Saha-So 2026) that establishes the query complexity of learning decision stumps.
item.dc:creator: Hadley Black, Arya Mazumdar, Barna Saha, Geelon So

item.title: Tiny Suffix Arrays
item.description: arXiv:2610.35543v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Suffix array and inverse suffix array queries on a text of length $n$ can be answered in $\widetilde{O}(\tau^3)$ time using an auxiliary data structure occupying $O(n/\tau)$ words, for any $\tau \in [1,n]$.
item.dc:creator: Sharma V. Thankachan

item.title: An $O(n^{0.1537})$-Coloring Algorithm for 3-Colorable Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.35859v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a polynomial-time randomized algorithm that colors every $n$-vertex $3$-colorable graph with $O(n^{0.1537})$ colors. This improves upon the previous bound of $O(n^{0.1954})$ colors by Bansal, Huang, and Lee (SODA '27). To achieve this result, we introduce a new algorithmic framework for finding a large independent set from a solution to the vector coloring SDP. Combined with the (combinatorial) dense-progress algorithm of Kawarabayashi, Thorup, and Yoneda (STOC '24), this framework yields an $n^{1/6 + o(1)}$-coloring algorithm. Furthermore, we strengthen the SDP-based algorithm specifically for 3-colorable graphs to achieve $O(n^{0.1537})$ colors.
item.dc:creator: Kaisei Deguchi, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Hirotaka Yoneda, Masataka Yoneda

item.title: Report the tolerance, not the count: exact phylogenetic distance deconvolution with incomplete references
item.description: arXiv:2610.30776v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Phylogenetic distance deconvolution represents mixture-to-reference distances by weighted sources placed on a reference tree. We study the minimum number of strictly interior sources that explains a distance profile, and what incomplete references cost. On a positive-rational reduced tree we give an exact algorithm with 2^O(K) poly(B) bit complexity for a free positive mean pendant and any nonempty set of observed leaves. With arbitrary missing references and a prescribed pendant the problem is W[1]-hard in the source budget K, even on positive binary trees supplied with a strict explanation using at most K+1 sources. We then use the algorithm as an instrument. Removing references can only lower the minimum source count, never raise it. The direction is a theorem at every error tolerance and held without exception in 23,545 draws, so which references are missing matters more than how many. Two adversarially chosen references suffice, at the median, to destroy uniqueness of the minimum explanation, and that number does not grow with panel size (Spearman 0.203, p = 0.15, over 20 to 353 references) where random loss scales linearly. Discarding 7,931 of 10,575 references from a real 16S panel at random costs 1.8% of the tolerance at which one source suffices. Discarding comparably many as whole clades costs 90%. That tolerance needs neither ground truth nor an error model, which makes the model measurable on real data. Published distance estimates exceed it in 296 of 296 cases. The mixture inferred by the published heuristic reproduces real observations better than the configuration that generated them in 282 of 296. The phenomenon is not unobservable in practice. It is unobservable through a point estimate of the count. Methods for this problem should report the tolerance at which an explanation of a given size exists.
item.dc:creator: Haotian Tang

item.title: Subgraph Isomorphism, Integer Linear Programming, and Lattices: A Linear Algebraic Framework
item.description: arXiv:2610.33235v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The subgraph isomorphism problem (SGI) asks a deceptively simple question: is a graph B found inside a parent graph A? Famously NP-complete and the subject of volumes of study, attempts to practically solve subgraph problems typically require specialized software or the focused application of problem-specific theoretical knowledge. Here we present a straightforward linear framework that neatly joins SGI to lattice theory and constrained satisfiability and, importantly, yields an easily implemented algorithm that naturally leverages consumer-grade hardware and off-the-shelf libraries to compete with state-of-the-art specialized solvers. We additionally show practical realizations in approachable settings, along with some benchmarks that reduce 6+ hour computations to seconds. Aimed at readability, we develop a series of computable algebraic invariants and demonstrate their application to familiar problems such as the Knight's Tour, with a focus on providing an accessible entry point for researchers in graph theory, abstract algebra, and students in general.
item.dc:creator: Bryant Gipson

item.title: A Factor-6 Truthful-in-Expectation Mechanism for Cascade Position Auctions
item.description: arXiv:2610.33707v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Position auctions require assigning advertisers to positions and determining their display order. Under cascade behavior, earlier clicks prevent users from reaching later placements, coupling the click probabilities of selected advertisements. Existing methods achieve constant-factor welfare approximation and monotone logarithmic-factor approximation separately, leaving open whether both guarantees can be attained simultaneously. The difficulty is that welfare-preserving rounding need not maintain the monotonicity of individual click-through rates required for truthful bidding. We resolve this problem by developing a polynomial-time randomized mechanism that achieves a factor-6 welfare approximation and truthfulness in expectation for arbitrary public advertiser-position click probabilities. The mechanism optimizes a reach-weighted linear relaxation and converts its solution into feasible ordered allocations through matching decomposition, probability-bounded grouping, and calibrated attenuation. This construction compensates for cascade dependence and ensures that each advertiser's expected click-through rate equals exactly one sixth of its fractional click coordinate. The resulting identity transfers the monotonicity of the fractional allocation to the implemented mechanism, enabling exact incentive-compatible payments while preserving the welfare guarantee. The allocation lottery and payments are computable in polynomial bit time, with exact sampling in expected polynomial time.
item.dc:creator: Qiuyu Chen, Baao Xie

item.title: Unconditional Lower Bounds for the Fredman--Khachiyan Algorithms for Monotone Boolean Duality Testing
item.description: arXiv:2610.34474v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove unconditional lower bounds on the number of recursive calls made by the two algorithms of Fredman and Khachiyan (1996) for monotone Boolean duality testing, as a function of the explicit input size $N$. For Algorithm A we show a lower bound of $N^{\Omega(\log N)}$ on the dual pairs $(\HH_k,\LL_k)$ obtained from the read-once family of Gurvich and Khachiyan. The proof lower-bounds the number of leaves of every binary decision tree computing the function by the modulus of its multilinear polynomial evaluated at a complex point of the unit circle. It therefore applies to every choice of branching variables and, more generally, to the class of two-child variable-restriction procedures whose terminal calls have polynomially bounded decision-tree complexity. On this family the number of calls is exactly $N^{\Theta(\log N)}$. For Algorithm B, a symmetric specialization of the polynomial padding construction of Kobayashi, Kurita, and Wasa, with full polynomial blocks, yields at least $q^{(t-1)k-t(t-1)/2}$ calls, where $k=4t^2$ and $q=\Theta(t^2)$; as a function of $N$ this is $N^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log N/\log\log N})}$ along an infinite family. In an appendix we show that applying the padding construction directly to Algorithm A gives $\Omega(2^n)$ calls on a dual pair obtained from an unsatisfiable $n$-variable formula, which is only $N^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log N/\log\log N})}$ in terms of the input size. No complexity-theoretic assumption is used. The proofs allow every branching-variable choice permitted by the respective algorithm. They concern the original recursive procedures, counting every invocation separately, without sharing calls or adding positive stopping tests.
item.dc:creator: Khaled Elbassioni

item.title: The Complexity of Value Optimization in Sporadic Task Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.34725v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Value-based Task Selection (VTS) asks whether a real-time system can select tasks whose total value reaches a required target while preserving every deadline. We study its threshold decision form for finite collections of independent sporadic tasks scheduled preemptively on one processor. We prove that this problem is $\Sigma_2^P$-complete for both constrained and arbitrary deadlines, even when all numerical parameters are encoded in unary. The existential choice is the selected task set, while the universal condition requires every processor-demand window to remain feasible. Our hardness reduction already uses constrained-deadline tasks. It represents universal assignments by Chinese Remainder Theorem timestamps and uses polynomial-weight local selector locks to enforce a valid existential assignment. The reduction produces polynomially many tasks, and every generated execution time, deadline, period, task value, and target is polynomially bounded in the source-instance size.
item.dc:creator: Christopher Harbourne, Nathan Fisher, Kecheng Yang, Pontus Ekberg, Sanjoy Baruah, Zhishan Guo

item.title: Attention under Bounded Key-Query Similarity: Space Complexity and Transformer Anisotropy
item.description: arXiv:2610.35020v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A growing body of work on KV-cache compression aims to reduce the memory requirements of autoregressive generation. These methods compress the stored context while approximately preserving attention computation, enabling generation with reduced memory consumption. Almost tight theoretical results on the worst case space complexity of attention have recently been obtained, but they are achieved by instances where queries can be perfectly aligned with keys. This directly contradicts the observed anisotropy of the key/query geometry in real transformers. In particular, it has been shown empirically that key/query cosine similarities are small even for most correlated pairs, i.e., near-perfect alignment of queries with keys does not happen in practice. In this paper, we study the space complexity of attention approximation under the assumption that key/query cosine similarities belong to a small interval around zero, i.e., a query cannot align too much with any key. We give a nearly space optimal algorithm and a corresponding space lower bound. Surprisingly, the distribution of key/query cosine similarities in our lower bound exhibits the anisotropy property empirically established and studied in the literature. Additionally, we show that the simple uniform sampling algorithm is nearly optimal for a typical range of parameters, supporting its surprising effectiveness on real datasets.
item.dc:creator: Justin Y. Chen, Ying Feng, Piotr Indyk, Michael Kapralov, Ekaterina Kochetkova, Boris Prokhorov

item.title: On the Number of Circuits in Regular Matroids (with Connections to Lattices and Codes)
item.description: arXiv:1807.05164v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that for any regular matroid on $m$ elements and any $\alpha \geq 1$, the number of $\alpha$-minimum circuits, or circuits whose size is at most an $\alpha$-multiple of the minimum size of a circuit in the matroid is bounded by $m^{O(\alpha^2)}$. This generalizes a result of Karger for the number of $\alpha$-minimum cuts in a graph. As a consequence, we obtain similar bounds on the number of $\alpha$-shortest vectors in "totally unimodular" lattices and on the number of $\alpha$-minimum weight codewords in "regular" codes.
item.dc:creator: Rohit Gurjar, Nisheeth K. Vishnoi

item.title: A New Test for Hamming-Weight Dependencies
item.description: arXiv:2108.13061v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We describe a new statistical test for pseudorandom number generators (PRNGs). Our test can find bias induced by dependencies among the Hamming weights of the outputs of a PRNG, even for PRNGs that pass state-of-the-art tests of the same kind from the literature, and in particular for generators based on $\mathbf F_2$-linear transformations such as the dSFMT, xoroshiro1024+, and WELL512a.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: ACM Transactions on Modeling and Computer Simulation, 32(3), 2022
item.dc:creator: David Blackman, Sebastiano Vigna

item.title: Optimal regret for dynamic matching with static priorities
item.description: arXiv:2503.09762v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study centralized two-way dynamic matching markets in which agents arrive stochastically over time and wait in queues associated with their types. We focus on static priority policies that assign each agent type a fixed ranking over its neighbors and make online matching decisions using only queue availability. We propose the General Priority ($\mathbf{GP}$) policy, which builds on the Tree Priority ($\mathbf{TP}$) policy introduced in [KAG25]. Under the general position gap condition, $\mathbf{GP}$ selects matches using a nondegenerate optimal basic solution of the fluid relaxation. It prioritizes children over parents within trees and consistently gives clockwise neighbors priority over counterclockwise neighbors on each cycle. We establish the optimal all-time regret scaling $O(\epsilon^{-1})$ for $\mathbf{GP}$ on general two-way matching networks, where the general position gap $\epsilon$ measures the fluid relaxation's distance from degeneracy. In particular, this resolves the conjecture by [KAG25] on the optimal $\epsilon$-dependence for $\mathbf{TP}$.
item.dc:creator: S\"uleyman Kerimov, Pengyu Qian, Mingwei Yang, Sophie H. Yu

item.title: Online Multi-Level Aggregation with Maximum Delay
item.description: arXiv:2608.06796v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study Multi-Level Aggregation with Maximum Delay (MLA-MD) on finite weighted rooted trees. Each service pays for a rooted subtree and for the maximum waiting time among the requests it clears. For the offline problem, we give an exact polynomial-time algorithm that computes both the optimum and an optimal service schedule. For the online problem, we give a deterministic $2$-competitive algorithm and, against an oblivious adversary, a randomized $e/(e-1)$-competitive algorithm. Both competitive ratios are optimal, even on rooted paths. We also extend the offline result and both online guarantees to service systems with submodular costs.
item.dc:creator: Tianhang Lu, Runtian Ren, Shengcai Liu, Ke Tang

item.title: Truly Work-efficient Parallel Deterministic $(\Delta+1)$-coloring and Maximal Independent Set
item.description: arXiv:2608.08296v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give deterministic parallel algorithms that compute a $(\Delta+1)$-coloring and a maximal independent set for a simple graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges in $O(n+m)$ work and $O(\mathrm{poly}\log n)$ depth.
item.dc:creator: Chase Hutton, Adam Melrod

item.title: A Near-Optimal Lower Bound for $\ell_p$-Subspace Embeddings, $1\leq p<2$
item.description: arXiv:2608.14201v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For $d \geq 2$, $p \geq 1$ and $\epsilon > 0$, let $N_p(d,\epsilon)$ be the smallest integer $N$ such that for every integer $n$ and every $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, there exists a matrix $\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n}$ satisfying $(1-\epsilon)\lVert Ax\rVert_p\leq \lVert\Phi A x\rVert_p\leq (1+\epsilon)\lVert Ax\rVert_p$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$. For every constant $p\geq 1$ with $p\not\in 2\mathbb{Z}$, when $d\gtrsim_p \log(1/\epsilon)$, the bound \[ N_p(d,\epsilon) \gtrsim_{p} \frac{d}{\epsilon^2 \operatorname{polylog}(d/\epsilon)} \] is established. This improves the previous lower bound $\Omega(1/(\epsilon^2\operatorname{polylog}(1/\epsilon)))$ due to Li et al. (SICOMP 2021) and is optimal up to logarithmic factors for $1\leq p<2$. The central technical idea originated from ChatGPT 6 Pro.
item.dc:creator: Yi Li

item.title: Exact algorithms for optimal discretization
item.description: arXiv:2608.25197v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The optimal discretization problem asks, given two disjoint sets of points $R$ and $B$ in the plane, for a minimal family of horizontal and vertical lines that separate the two sets, so that no cell delimited by the lines contains points from both sets. The problem arises as a pre-processing in supervised machine learning, and has received significant attention in parameterized algorithmics. Answering the question raised by Bonnet, Giannopoulos, and Lampis [IPEC 2017] and Froese [PhD thesis, 2018], it was shown by Kratsch, Masa\v{r}\'ik, Muzi, Pilipczuk, and Sorge [SODA 2021] that optimal discretization admits a fixed-parameter algorithm with running time $2^{\mathcal{O}(k^2 \log k)} \cdot n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$, where $k$ is the solution size and $n = |R| + |B|$. In this paper we give an algorithm for optimal discretization that runs in time $\mathcal{O}(1.9602^n)$. We also study the related point separation problem that asks to separate all input points by axis-parallel lines. For this problem we obtain an algorithm with runtime $\mathcal{O}(1.8899^n)$. Our guarantees follow from structural observations about bichromatic and monochromatic point sets. To our knowledge, these are the first improvements over the trivial $2^n$ bound for both problems.
item.dc:creator: L\'aszl\'o Kozma, Junqi Tan

item.title: Prefix Sharing Is a Sorting Problem
item.description: arXiv:2609.13692v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM serving reuses KV cache by exact prefix match, so when a prompt is assembled from a set of reusable pieces -- retrieved passages, tool definitions, few-shot exemplars -- the order chosen for those pieces determines how much computation can be shared. Every deployed system fixes that order by a single global convention. We prove this is optimal only when requests contain at most two pieces, and asymptotically wrong in general. Our main result is a structure theorem: the minimum prefix-trie cost equals min_H sum_x w(x) t_x(H) over binary hierarchies H on the requests, where t_x(H) is the canonical decomposition size of the set of requests needing chunk x. Choosing chunk orders is therefore equivalent to choosing one hierarchy over requests. The identity yields an O(3^m) exact algorithm, identifies the two-chunk case as minimum vertex cover, and shows that on the leave-one-out family the optimum is the minimum external path length of a binary tree -- the merge-sort recursion -- so a global order pays Theta(n^2) against a true cost of Theta(n log n). Agglomerative clustering by common intersection is a tight 1/2-approximation for the achievable saving. On BM25 retrieval traces over three BEIR corpora the resulting layout reduces prefill by 17-36% against production RAG ordering, and the margin widens with retrieval depth as the theory predicts. Serving requests in the hierarchy's DFS order finally lets a cache holding one request's context attain the unbounded-cache optimum exactly, so cache capacity and reorder window act as substitutes.
item.dc:creator: Rong He

item.title: Geometry-Dependent Approximation for Non-Monotone $k$-Submodular Maximization
item.description: arXiv:2610.04049v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the maximization of a nonnegative $k$-submodular function, not assumed monotone, in which each of $n$ elements receives one of $k\ge2$ labels or stays unselected and the selected elements must satisfy a constraint. For a compact convex down-closed region $P\subseteq[0,1]^n$ of fractional selection vectors, the diagonal level $\zeta(P)=\max\{t\in[0,1]:t(1,\ldots,1)\in P\}$ is the largest selection probability that can be given to all elements at once; it equals $r/n$ for a uniform matroid of rank $r$, and $\zeta(P)=1$ means that the constraint is vacuous. We give approximation coefficients that increase continuously with $\zeta$. They come from one inequality for the multilinear extension of the objective: the algorithm computes an action without querying the objective, and objective feedback gives a comparator-independent update direction. For $k\ge3$, feasibility of the action reduces to three polynomial inequalities in one variable; for $k=2$ the profile is closed form. At $\zeta=0$ the coefficients are $0.4456\ldots$ for $k=2$ and $0.4541\ldots$ for every $k\ge3$. For every finite $k\ge3$ they reach $1/2$ above an explicit level, which is $0.4026\ldots$ for $k=3,4,5$, and at $\zeta=1$ they reach $1/2$ for $k=2$, $(\sqrt{17}-3)/2$ for $k=3,4$, and $k/(2k-1)$ for $k\ge5$. Online linear optimization gives $O(\sqrt T)$ approximate regret, with gradient feedback or with value queries made after each action. The coefficients carry over to matroids, with expected and high-probability guarantees, and to any fixed number of knapsacks: the zero-level coefficients hold on every instance, and the larger ones when items are small or when prefix enumeration keeps the diagonal level on one branch. For one budget the enumeration exponent is $O(1/\varepsilon)$.
item.dc:creator: Vaneet Aggarwal

item.title: A deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for the Bilu--Linial signing problem on bipartite graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.09972v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for the Bilu--Linial signing problem on bipartite graphs. For every finite simple bipartite graph of maximum degree at most an integer $\Delta\ge3$, the algorithm assigns signs to its edges so that the signed adjacency matrix has operator norm strictly less than $2\sqrt{\Delta-1}$. Our algorithm builds on the randomized recursive repair framework of Jadbabaie, Saberi, and Sra~\cite{JSS26}, with deterministic rules for sign selection and vertex deletion.
item.dc:creator: Zhiqiang Xu

item.title: 0.4633-Approximation for Online and Offline on-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization
item.description: arXiv:2610.21072v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We obtain the approximation coefficient $\alpha_0=54440750000/117486474169>0.463378$ for maximizing nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed subsets of the unit cube, with queries allowed throughout the cube. This improves the previous best coefficient, $4/9$. A coordinatewise map, exponential on small coordinates and linear-fractional on large ones, turns the learner's state, a feasible point, into a feasible action whose value is at least $\alpha_0$ times that of any feasible point, up to a linear term. The proof is analytical and reduces to one-dimensional inequalities. The linear term has an unbiased estimator from one noisy-gradient query, so online maximization reduces to linear learning. Under a uniform bound on the gradients, the expected approximate regret is $O(\sqrt T)$ with projected ascent and $O(T^{3/4})$ with one linear-maximization call per round; with one noisy value per round, it is $O(T^{3/4})$ and $O(T^{7/8})$. Online-to-batch conversion gives offline guarantees. With exact values and gradients, contracting the objective toward a feasible interior point yields an expected $(\alpha_0-\varepsilon)$-approximation for every nonnegative $C^1$ DR-submodular objective, with oracle counts polynomial in $n$ and $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and no gradient or smoothness parameter. Sampling and standard rounding give $(\alpha_0-\varepsilon)$-approximation for submodular set functions under one matroid or a fixed number of knapsack constraints.
item.dc:creator: Vaneet Aggarwal, Donglei Du

item.title: Amplified Pruning and Path Selectors for Deterministic Radio Gossiping
item.description: arXiv:2610.28930v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study deterministic gossiping in unknown strongly connected directed radio networks with $n$ vertices, $m$ arcs, and distinct identifiers in $[N]$, where $N=n^{\mathcal O(1)}$. Messages are unrestricted and collision detection is unavailable. Our neighborhood-clearing procedure reuses an elected receiver to secure its entire closed in-neighborhood in $\mathcal O(n\log^2n\log\log n)$ rounds. Charging each distinct closed neighborhood once yields $\mathcal O(m\log^2n\log\log n)$ rounds under an explicit degree-concentration condition, for every polynomial identifier range. A complementary adaptive-pruning procedure combines quadratic contraction with completion sensitive to the number of unsecured sources. If $a\ge1$ sources remain at completion entry, permutation selectors reduce the balanced completion budget by a factor of $\log^{2/3}(a+1)$ relative to interleaved path selectors. A geometric execution attains $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(k^2+n\tau+\min\{u^2,(nu)^{2/3}\})$ for a path cover of scale $k$, weight $\tau$, and $u$ exceptions. For directed graphs with common in- and out-degree $\Delta$, the portfolio achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n\sqrt\Delta,n^2/\Delta\})$. Every graph also admits $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n^{4/3},N+(mn)^{3/5}\})$ rounds. Only $n,N$ are inputs; degrees, covers, and structural constants are used solely in the analysis. The unrestricted polynomial-identifier density extension remains open.
item.dc:creator: Qin Xin

item.title: Single-Machine Guarantees on Unrelated Machines and Beyond: Proportional Fairness for Nonclairvoyant Polytope Scheduling
item.description: arXiv:2610.32545v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Polytope Scheduling Problem (PSP) is a general framework for preemptive scheduling in which feasible instantaneous job allocations form a packing polytope. In the nonclairvoyant online setting, Proportional Fairness (PF), a practical allocation rule rooted in market theory, is the leading general-purpose algorithm. On a single machine, PF coincides with weighted Round-Robin, which is $2$-competitive for weighted completion time with uniform release dates (optimal for nonclairvoyant algorithms) and $(2+\varepsilon)$-speed $O(1/\varepsilon)$-competitive for weighted flow time. Known guarantees beyond a single machine are weaker. This raises a central question: Are these heterogeneous environments intrinsically harder than a single machine under nonclairvoyance? We show that they are not: PF retains both single-machine guarantees on the novel class of support-submodular polytopes, which includes unrelated machines and polymatroids. On unrelated machines, this refutes a belief (JACM'18, SODA'25) that PF is not $O(1)$-speed $O(1)$-competitive for weighted flow time. Our main technical contribution is an equivalent characterization: a polytope is support submodular if and only if, for all job weights, the optimal weighted completion time is concave in the processing requirements. This structural insight underlies both guarantees. For general PSP, the picture changes: we give the first lower bound above $2$, showing that every randomized nonclairvoyant algorithm has a competitive ratio of at least $2+10^{-5}$ for weighted completion time, even with uniform release dates. On the positive side, we substantially improve the best known guarantee for weighted completion time from $27$ (SICOMP'26) to $4$ via a new dual-fitting analysis of PF. For weighted flow time, we show that PF achieves the first $O(1)$-speed $O(1)$-competitive nonclairvoyant guarantee for graph scheduling.
item.dc:creator: Sven J\"ager, Alexander Lindermayr, Bart Zondervan

item.title: k-SUM Hardness Implies Treewidth-SETH
item.description: arXiv:2510.08185v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that if k-SUM is hard, in the sense that the standard algorithm is essentially optimal, then a variant of the SETH called the Primal Treewidth SETH is true. Formally: if there is an $\varepsilon>0$ and an algorithm which solves SAT in time $(2-\varepsilon)^{tw}|\phi|^{O(1)}$, where $tw$ is the width of a given tree decomposition of the primal graph of the input, then there exists a randomized algorithm which solves k-SUM in time $n^{(1-\delta)\frac{k}{2}}$ for some $\delta>0$ and all sufficiently large $k$. We also establish an analogous result for the k-XOR problem, where integer addition is replaced by component-wise addition modulo $2$. As an application of our reduction we are able to revisit tight lower bounds on the complexity of several fundamental problems parameterized by treewidth (Independent Set, Max Cut, $k$-Coloring). Our results imply that these bounds, which were initially shown under the SETH, also hold if one assumes the k-SUM or k-XOR Hypotheses, arguably increasing our confidence in their validity.
item.dc:creator: Michael Lampis

item.title: Tensor Decomposition for Non-Clifford Gate Minimization
item.description: arXiv:2602.15285v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires substantial resources for non-Clifford gates. Their count also enters exponentially into the runtime of several classical simulation methods. We present algebraic methods for minimizing the non-Clifford CCZ (Toffoli) count in {CNOT,CCZ} phase circuits using tensor decomposition over $\mathbb{F}_2$. On standard cubic benchmarks, these methods match or improve prior automated Toffoli counts, with most instances optimized in under a minute on a single CPU. With additional computation, the decompositions provide effective initializations for existing T-count methods, improving T counts on several circuits. We also present algebraic methods for CNOT-count optimization at fixed Toffoli count. This gives competitive ancilla-free finite-field multiplication circuits and reduces the CNOT count of XOR AES S-box circuits.
item.dc:creator: Kirill Khoruzhii, Patrick Gel{\ss}, Sebastian Pokutta

item.title: Faster Parallel Batch-Dynamic Algorithms for Low Out-Degree Orientation
item.description: arXiv:2602.17811v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A low out-degree orientation directs each edge of an undirected graph with the goal of minimizing the maximum out-degree of a vertex. In the parallel batch-dynamic setting, one can insert or delete batches of edges, and the goal is to process the entire batch in parallel with work per edge similar to that of a single sequential update and with span (or depth) for the entire batch that is polylogarithmic. In this paper we present work-efficient parallel batch-dynamic algorithms for maintaining a low out-degree orientation of an undirected graph, both in the amortized and worst-case settings. All results herein achieve polylogarithmic depth; the focus of this paper is on minimizing the work, which varies across results. In the amortized setting, we give a parallel batch-dynamic algorithm that maintains a $O(c)$-orientation in $O(\log n)$ work per update in expectation, where $c$ is a known upper bound on the arboricity over the update sequence. Our algorithm has optimal work in expectation. This result is the parallelization of the classic dynamic orientation algorithm of Brodal and Fagerberg [WADS '99], and, in this setting, is a logarithmic factor faster than the best prior parallel amortized algorithm of Liu et al. [SPAA '22]. In the worst-case setting, we give an $O(c+\log n)$-orientation with worst-case expected work per update $O(\log n)$. This is work-efficient, matching the best known sequential dynamic work of Berglin and Brodal [Algorithmica '20], and implies the existence of an $O(c)$-orientation algorithm with $O(\log^2 n)$ worst-case expected work per update. Both of our algorithms also have deterministic bounds with an additional logarithmic factor in the work. Similar to Berglin and Brodal, by adjusting the parameters of our worst-case algorithm, we achieve tradeoffs where the work is faster than $O(\log n)$ in expectation per update but the max out-degree is worse.
item.dc:creator: Guy Blelloch, Andrew Brady, Laxman Dhulipala, Jeremy Fineman, Kishen Gowda, Chase Hutton

item.title: List coloring uncrowded hypergraphs at the shattering threshold
item.description: arXiv:2606.18048v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Improving an earlier bound of Frieze and Mubayi, Iliopoulos showed that any $k$-uniform uncrowded hypergraph of maximum degree $\Delta$ has list chromatic number at most $(1+o(1))(k-1)\Big(\frac{\Delta}{\log\Delta}\Big)^{\frac{1}{k-1}}$. Determining the optimal leading constant in this bound remains a major open problem. A natural target for the constant, suggested by the coupon-collector heuristic, is $(k-1)^{\frac{1}{k-1}}$, which also arises independently as the shattering threshold for coloring and finding large independent sets in sparse random hypergraphs. We show that uncrowded hypergraphs attain this threshold: for $k \ge 2$, every $k$-uniform uncrowded hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ of maximum degree at most $\Delta$ satisfies $$\chi_\ell(\mathcal{H})\le(1+o(1))\Big((k-1)\frac{\Delta}{\log\Delta}\Big)^{\frac{1}{k-1}}.$$ This matches the coupon-collector heuristic, and establishes a 2019 conjecture of Molloy for uncrowded hypergraphs. As a consequence, we show that every $k$-uniform linear hypergraph of maximum degree at most $\Delta$ has chromatic number at most $c_k\Big(\frac{\Delta}{\log \Delta}\Big)^{\frac{1}{k-1}}$ with $c_k=1-o_k(1)$, resolving, in a stronger form, a recent conjecture of Verstra\"ete and Wilson on the independence number of linear hypergraphs. Our techniques yield the first palette sparsification result for hypergraph coloring using $o(\Delta^{\frac{1}{k-1}})$ colors per vertex. Specifically, for an uncrowded $k$-graph $\mathcal{H}$ and $q=\Theta\Big({\Big(\frac{\Delta}{\gamma\log\Delta}\Big)^{\frac{1}{k-1}}}\Big)$, sampling $\Theta(\Delta^{\frac{\gamma}{k-1}})$ colors per vertex suffices to obtain a proper $q$-coloring of $\mathcal{H}$ w.h.p. As an algorithmic consequence, we obtain a single-pass streaming algorithm using $O\big(n^{1+o(1)}\big)$ space for uncrowded $k$-graphs, and, via hypergraph partitioning, for linear hypergraphs as well.
item.dc:creator: Abhishek Dhawan, Abhishek Methuku, Minh-Quan Vo
